questions.prompt: What happens if you declare two interfaces with the same name?

options.text: TypeScript merges them into a single interface containing all their members
The second one replaces the first

questions.explanation: Interface declaration merging combines same-named interfaces into one type with all members — the basis of module augmentation.

questions.prompt: Can `type` aliases be merged like interfaces?

options.text: No — a duplicate `type` name is an error; only interfaces (and namespaces) merge

questions.explanation: Type aliases don't merge; declaring the same alias twice is an error. Merging works on interfaces and namespaces.

questions.prompt: How do you add a typed property to a third-party module's interface?

options.text: Module augmentation: declare module 'lib' { interface X { ... } } in a file that's a module

questions.explanation: Module augmentation reopens a library's interface via declare module and merges your members into it — no source edits or casts.

questions.prompt: How do you add a typed property to `window`?

options.text: Inside a module, declare global { interface Window { ... } }

questions.explanation: declare global inside a module merges new members into the global Window interface — the typed alternative to casting.

questions.prompt: An augmentation file that isn't already a module needs a top-level `______ {}` to make it one. (one keyword)
questions.explanation: Adding `export {}` turns a file into a module, which is required for declare global and scoped module augmentation.

questions.prompt: Where do namespaces still make sense?

options.text: For organizing all application code instead of modules
For merging extra members onto a function/class/enum value, and in ambient .d.ts files describing global libraries
They are fully removed from TypeScript

questions.explanation: ES modules replaced namespaces for app code. Namespaces remain useful for value merging and ambient global (script-loaded) library typings.
